title: Manitoba Website Accessibility Law
description: Manitoba's information and communication standard: since May 1, 2025, businesses and non-profits with one employee must meet WCAG 2.1 AA on new web content.
h1: Website accessibility law in Manitoba: WCAG 2.1 for businesses of every size
name: Manitoba
lead: Manitoba has the widest-reaching website rule for private organizations of any province we checked. Since May 1, 2025, any business or non-profit with one or more employees in Manitoba must make new web content, and content needed to buy its goods or services, meet WCAG 2.1 Level AA.

facts.label: Regulation
facts.value: Accessible Information and Communication Standard Regulation, Manitoba Regulation 47/2022

facts.label: Who it applies to
facts.value: Any other organization subject to The Accessibility for Manitobans Act that has one or more employees in Manitoba

facts.label: Start date for businesses and non-profits
Standard
facts.value: WCAG 2.1 Level AA, at a minimum

facts.label: Web content covered
facts.value: Content published on or after the day the regulation applies to you, and content required to access your goods and services

facts.label: Web applications covered
facts.value: Those published or given a significant update (a change to functionality, user base or purpose) on or after that day

facts.label: Exceptions
facts.value: Not technically feasible; technology not readily available; undue hardship; no direct control over the content; product labels or other product information

facts.label: Intranets
facts.value: Covered only for government departments and listed public sector bodies, not for businesses

facts.label: Criteria WCAG 2.1 added over 2.0 (examples)
facts.value: Reflow (1.4.10, AA), Non-text Contrast (1.4.11, AA), Text Spacing (1.4.12, AA), Label in Name (2.5.3, A)

facts.label: Extra duty at 50 or more employees
facts.value: Keep a written record of accessibility and training policies and tell the public they are available on request

sections.h2: Why Manitoba's rule reaches almost every business
body: Manitoba phased the Accessible Information and Communication Standard Regulation in over three years. Government departments came first, then agencies, health authorities, larger cities, schools and libraries. The last group, reached on May 1, 2025, is described in the regulation as any other organization subject to the Act that has one or more employees in Manitoba.

The Manitoba Accessibility Office spells out who that means: shops, restaurants, hotels, legal, healthcare and other professional services, and non-profits such as charities, unions, community organizations, places of worship and member associations. There is no size threshold for the website requirement. A two-person bookkeeping office with a website is in scope.
Size matters only for paperwork. At 50 or more employees you keep a written record of your accessibility and training policies and let the public know they are available on request.

sections.h2: What content has to meet WCAG 2.1 Level AA
body: The web content section is built on two triggers. Content published on or after the day the regulation applied to you must meet WCAG 2.1 Level AA. So must any content required to access your goods and services, no matter when it was published. That second trigger is the one owners miss: an old booking form, a product page or a donation form that customers rely on is covered even if it predates 2025.

Web applications have their own rule. A web application is software that runs on a web server and is used through a browser, such as a client portal or an online ordering tool. It must meet WCAG 2.1 Level AA if it was published, or received a significant update, after your start date. A significant update is one that changes its functionality, user base or purpose.

Note the version. Ontario's rule is WCAG 2.0; Manitoba's is 2.1, which adds criteria aimed at mobile and low-vision users: Reflow (content that fits a narrow screen without sideways scrolling), Non-text Contrast (icons and form borders you can see), Text Spacing, and Label in Name (the accessible name matches the visible label).

The regulation lets content fall short of WCAG 2.1 Level AA if it is not technically feasible, if the technology needed is not readily available, if meeting the standard would cause undue hardship, if you do not have direct control over the content, or if it relates to product labels or other product information.

The direct-control exception helps with embedded third-party tools such as a booking widget or a map you cannot change. It does not cover a theme or template you chose and can replace. The regulation does not explain how undue hardship is measured, so treat it as a last resort and write down your reasoning if you rely on it.

The standard is about information and communication in general, not just code. You must let the public and employees know they can request information in an accessible format or with a communication support, and when someone asks, consult them, then provide it in a timely way at no extra cost. You also need a feedback process about accessible communication.

Training is part of it. The regulation lists the people who must be trained, including anyone who develops or maintains your web content and anyone who buys information technology or communication tools. If an outside agency edits your site, ask how they train their staff, and train the employee who posts your news and events.

stepsHeading: Bringing a Manitoba site into line

steps.name: Find the task pages
steps.text: List every page a customer needs to buy, book, donate, register or get support. These are covered whatever their age.

steps.name: Test against 2.1, not 2.0
steps.text: Include the criteria WCAG 2.1 added, such as Reflow, Non-text Contrast and Label in Name, alongside the basics like alt text and keyboard access.

steps.name: Post the notice
steps.text: Add a short statement to the site that information is available in accessible formats on request, with a contact that someone checks.

steps.name: Train who publishes
steps.text: Give staff who edit the site, and staff who buy software, accessible communication training and keep a record of it.

checklist: Your online booking, checkout or donation form works with a keyboard and a screen reader.
Pages still read cleanly when the browser is zoomed far in.
Icons and input borders are visible against their background.
Your site says how to ask for information in another format.
There is a way to give feedback about accessible communication.
New PDFs and posters on the site have a text equivalent.

faqs.q: We only have three employees. Do we really have to meet WCAG 2.1?
faqs.a: Yes, for content published since May 1, 2025 and for content people need to access your goods and services. The regulation applies to organizations with one or more employees in Manitoba.

faqs.q: Does our old blog need fixing?
faqs.a: Not if it was published before your start date and is not needed to access your goods and services. New posts are covered.

faqs.q: Our booking system is a third-party widget. Are we responsible for it?
faqs.a: The regulation excuses content you do not have direct control over. You still control the choice of vendor, so ask them for their accessibility conformance and consider switching at renewal.

faqs.q: Is there a compliance report like Ontario's?
faqs.a: The Manitoba Accessibility Office pages we checked do not describe a compliance report for businesses. The duties are to meet the standard and keep records if you have 50 or more employees.
